INTEREST OF THE AMICI CURIAE1
Amici are public health organizations, researchers, lawyers, and professionals focused on promoting
evidence-based solutions to reduce injury and death,
particularly from gun violence. They have a strong interest in ensuring that this Court’s Second Amendment analysis is informed by empirical public health
research. Many of them have participated as amici curiae in previous cases before this Court involving firearm restrictions. See, e.g., United States v. Rahimi,
602 U.S. 680 (2024);  New York State Rifle & Pistol
Ass’n v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022); United States v. Castleman, 572 U.S. 157 (2014); and McDonald v. City of
Chicago, 561 U.S. 742 (2010).
As public health organizations and professionals,
amici are well-suited to assist the Court in understanding the evidence related to assault weapons and
how that evidence illuminates the analysis required
by Bruen. To that end, amici highlight the pertinent
primary sources and secondary scholarship that are
vital to addressing firearm regulation.
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The Constitution’s Framers never had to confront
mass carnage perpetrated by a single individual.
When the Second Amendment was adopted, guns
were less advanced and ill-suited for committing mass
murder. Now, however, a single individual intent on

causing maximum devastation can acquire a firearm
designed for military use and fire hundreds of highvelocity rounds in a matter of minutes—at school children, faith congregations, law enforcement, or ordinary Americans at the local grocery store. Horrifically, shootings of that sort have become all too common.
To address this growing problem, Cook County
and Connecticut enacted evidence-based legislation
prohibiting possession of assault weapons, like the
AR-15 at issue here, that are favored by mass shooters
and better suited for war. The Court should uphold
the constitutionality of those regulations.
First, to help ground the Court’s decision, amici
examine scholarship that reveals the unique risks
posed by assault weapons and the success of regulations—like those at issue here—at reducing violence
and mass shootings.
Second, amici apply both steps of the Second
Amendment framework set by this Court in District of
Columbia v. Heller , 554 U.S. 570 (2008); Bruen;
Rahimi; and Wolford v. Lopez, 609 U.S. 185 (2026).
At step one, this Court’s precedent supports finding that military-grade weaponry, such as AR-15s, are
outside the scope of “Arms” covered by the Second
Amendment.
At step two, a thorough review of the historical
record and primary and secondary scholarship shows
that the challenged laws are relevantly similar to frequently enacted and upheld historical regulations of
unusually dangerous weapons.  The regulations at issue are also relevantly analogous to restrictions imposed on armed groups during the colonial period and
into the nineteenth century. That matters because, in

3


the Founding Era, only groups were capable of inflicting the sort of mass carnage that a single individual
wielding an assault rifle can now produce in minutes.
And just as armed groups and unusually dangerous
weapons could be regulated two centuries ago to protect the public, so assault weapons should be subject
to regulation today.
ARGUMENT
I. Gun Violence Is a Public Health Crisis.
A. Mass Casualty Events Caused by Single
Individuals Wielding Firearms Are a
New Phenomenon.
As the American Medical Association has declared, gun violence is a “public health crisis.” 2 Gun
violence—specifically, high-casualty mass shootings
perpetrated by a single individual—is a uniquely modern public health crisis that affects the well-being and
safety of all Americans. To put this case in context, we
briefly highlight what is at stake.
The Founders had no occasion to consider mass
shootings perpetrated by individuals. Homicides with
firearms were relatively rare, and mass killings were
both rare and required the participation of armed
groups, as societal and technological realities were
materially different when the Second Amendment
was adopted.
Firearms prevalent at the Founding generally
held one round and took even skilled operators

Given the less advanced nature of early weapons,
mass killings prior to the mid-nineteenth century
were perpetrated by groups of assailants, rather than
lone actors. “The only way to kill a large number of
people was to rally like-minded neighbors and go on a
rampage with * * * weapons that were certainly lethal
but did not provide individuals or small groups of people the means to inflict mass casualties on their own.”8
As a consequence, Founding-era firearms technology

found that 33% of mass shootings in our Nation’s history occurred after 2010. 11 The lethality of mass

The public health approach to preventing gun violence addresses both firearm access and the underlying factors that contribute to gun violence. It uses a
comprehensive approach like those that have been
successfully employed over the last century to eradicate diseases like smallpox and reduce deaths due to
smoking and motor vehicle crashes.
Fundamentally, public health aims to address the
underlying causes of a disease or injury before they
can occur to control and reduce the spread of outbreaks. It looks impartially for commonalities behind
outbreaks and considers factors that could lead to a
different result. Overwhelmingly, one commonality
behind high-casualty mass shootings is a type of firearm that enables an individual to kill and injure dozens of victims within minutes. Restricting the possession of this particular weapon type both comports with
the accepted and effective public health approach and
is well within the States’ traditional police power.
This is precisely what Respondents here have done.
B. Public Health Research Demonstrates
the Dangerousness of Assault Weapons.
Assault weapons, like the AR-15 at issue here, enable a single person to inflict mass carnage in
minutes. E.g., Sandy Hook Elementary School (26
deaths, under 5 minutes); Marjory Stoneman Douglas

8


High School (17 deaths, 6 minutes); Route 91 Harvest
Festival (60 deaths, 11 minutes).16
Public health research shows both that assault
weapons are frequently used in mass shootings and
that their use results in greater fatalities and injuries.
Multiple studies also demonstrate that assaultweapon regulations are associated with reductions in
both the number and lethality of mass shootings, illustrating that it is assault weapons in particular that
are unusually dangerous. We highlight these research
findings below but first pause to explain the value of
public health research.
1.  Importance of Rigorous Public
Health Research.
Reliable research is essential to understanding
the factors that contribute to deaths and injuries and
to the systematic evaluation of the effects of related
policies. Such research is anchored in careful use of
data and methodological design. Public health studies
typically undergo peer review by experts before publication; courts should be cautious of relying on nonpeer-reviewed materials, as this step ensures the use

To develop a valid understanding of the public
health effects of laws, researchers need to use scientifically sound measures of both the operative legal
provisions and the outcome(s) being studied. For research evaluating state and federal gun laws, this is
predicated on carefully defined statutory language
and analysis of high-quality outcome data. All research studies are subject to limitations, and disclosure of these limitations is an expected element of all
published manuscripts.
Although there is strong research demonstrating
the dangerousness of assault weapons and the effects
of related laws, these findings must be understood in
the context of challenges faced by all research on these
topics. First, there are variations among available datasets’ definitions of “mass shooting.” Second, state
and federal laws often use different operative definitions of “assault weapon,” making it challenging to examine effects across multiple jurisdictions.17

Moreover, the specific conduct regulated by these
laws has also varied across jurisdictions. The Federal
Assault Weapons Ban (“FAWB”), for example, prohibited the manufacture, transfer, or possession of semiautomatic assault weapons—but it exempted assault
weapons that were possessed prior to the enactment
date. Pub. L. No. 103-322, § 110102(b), 108 Stat. 1796.
Many state laws that generally prohibit the possession of assault weapons included similar grandfathering clauses. Some states do not prohibit possession at
all, but prohibit manufacture, sale, or transfer, or
make possession contingent on acquiring a license.
Additionally, many assault weapons laws did not go
into effect immediately, allowing for a pre-effective
date surge in purchase of such weapons. These variations can pose challenges for researchers seeking to
estimate the effects of these laws across states.18

to federal restrictions. For example, some data is
available only to law enforcement and some data
tracks firearms generally, but not assault weapons

there are numerous peer-reviewed public health studies demonstrating that assault weapons pose exceptional risks to public safety. In fact, given these limitations on the research, the unusual dangerousness of
these lethal weapons may, if anything, be understated.

II. Regulating Assault Weapons Is Consistent
With History And Tradition.
A. The Bruen Framework.
In Bruen, the Court set out the two-part Second
Amendment test. At step one, the challenger must
prove that “the Second Amendment’s plain text covers
an individual’s conduct,” in which case “the Constitution presumptively protects that conduct.” Bruen, 597
U.S. at 24. At step two, the government must demonstrate that the regulation is “consistent with the principles that underpin our regulatory tradition.”
Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 692.
To do so, the state can show that the modern restriction is sufficiently analogous to historical regulations. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 29-30 . When using analogical reasoning, courts are instructed to focus on “how
and why the regulations burden a law-abiding citizen’s right to armed self-defense.” Ibid. at 29. The
“how” is the manner in which a restriction is achieved;
the “why” is the motivation or interest behind the restriction. Id. Critically, the Court emphasized that
when the regulation implicates “unprecedented societal concerns or dramatic technological changes,” the
historical analysis requires “a more nuanced approach.” Id. at 27.
The AR-15—or, more generally, firearms allowing
a single individual to perpetrate mass carnage—are
unique to the modern era, as described above. As such,
the regulations challenged in these cases have no “historical twin.” Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 692. The “unprecedented societal concerns and dramatic technological
changes” presented by these weapons therefore are
precisely the circumstances that invite this “more nuanced approach.” Bruen, 597 U.S. at 26-27. The Bruen

restricting the possession of “dangerous and unusual

many States, including Maine, Massachusetts, Florida, and North Carolina, sustained the tradition of restricting armed groups to address the risk of mass violence by adopting laws prohibiting armed groups
from acting as private militias. Frassetto, supra, at
59-68.58 This unbroken tradition continues today with
all 50 States, through state constitutions or statutes,
prohibiting private, unauthorized militias. These historical laws and the laws at issue in this case both
seek to address the same harm—the prevention or
mitigation mass violence—by restricting the means by
which it was achieved.
Whether under Bruen step one or step two;
whether under a straightforward historical analysis
or a “more nuanced approach,” the regulations enacted in Cook County and Connecticut address a modern crisis through use of restrictions that are consistent with the Second Amendment. Like regulations
adopted and enforced in earlier centuries, the assault
weapon rules challenged here address unusually dangerous weapons with the capacity for inflicting mass
violence—and do so through relevantly similar
means. As Justice Barrett observed in Wolford, “too
narrow” a focus on the proffered analogs risks ignoring that “[t]oday, the right to bear arms is misused in
other ways that were unknown to our forebears.” 609
